title: Quantum Computation for Pricing Caps using the LIBOR Market Model
abstract_summary: This preprint develops a quantum computing approach to price interest-rate caps under the LIBOR Market Model by integrating quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) into Monte Carlo simulations. The authors propose a hybrid classical-quantum workflow that applies QAE to the expectation for the final tenor, demonstrate quantum circuit constructions for distribution loading and payoff estimation, and show improved convergence compared to purely classical Monte Carlo in their numerical experiments.
methodology_description: The paper develops and evaluates a hybrid classical-quantum pipeline to price interest-rate caps under the LIBOR Market Model (LMM). They (i) calibrate the LMM using market-implied volatilities (assuming piecewise-constant instantaneous volatilities as in Brigo & Mercurio), (ii) simulate forward LIBOR rates via classical Monte Carlo using the GBM solution for each forward rate (discretized annually, Fi(T+Δ)=Fi(T)·exp(√Δ·σi·Zi − ½σi^2Δ)), and (iii) compare three pricing methods: (a) pure classical Monte Carlo for all caplets, (b) a quantum-classical hybrid in which forward rates are simulated classically up to the second-last alive tenor and quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE, specifically an iterative QAE / IQAE) is applied to estimate the expectation for the final tenor, and (c) a pure-quantum approach that loads multivariate distributions of all caplets into separate quantum registers and applies QAE to the joint distribution. Quantum subroutines include distribution loading into amplitude-encoded log-normal states, comparator circuits to mark payoff conditions, Ry rotations to map payoff values into amplitudes, and IQAE to estimate expected payoff amplitudes (avoiding full QFT-based QAE). The Black-76 formula (under LMM-consistent volatilities) is used as the theoretical benchmark. Experiments vary the number of Monte Carlo simulations and the number of qubits used for distribution discretization; results are compared via estimated cap prices, absolute estimation error, sample means, and confidence intervals over multiple trials.
algorithms_used: Classical Monte Carlo simulation (Geometric Brownian Motion per forward rate)
Quantum state preparation / distribution loading (amplitude encoding)
Comparator circuits and amplitude encoding of payoff
dataset_used: Benchmark forward rates and implied volatilities from Brigo & Mercurio (2006) were used as the market dataset / model parameters (piecewise-constant instantaneous volatilities and an initial forward LIBOR curve, e.g. initial LIBOR ≈ 4.69% in examples). A 3-year cap example (tenor T = {1,2,3}) and longer-tenor examples (T = 3, 6, 10) using the same benchmark parameterization were evaluated.

experiment_input.preprocessing: No external preprocessing reported beyond using the LMM calibration assumption (piecewise-constant instantaneous volatilities) to obtain per-caplet Black-76 volatilities. Forward rates are simulated via GBM discretization; distributions for final-tenor forward rates are discretized / amplitude-encoded into 2^n states per register.

pipeline_steps: Calibrate LMM instantaneous volatilities using market-implied caplet volatilities (assume piecewise-constant vol table).
Generate forward-rate paths classically via Monte Carlo: simulate Fi(t) as GBM using Eq. Fi(T) = Fi(t)·exp(∫σ dZ − ½∫σ^2 dt); in practice time-step Δ = 1 year.
Method A (Classical MC): compute caplet payoffs and discount/sum to produce cap price.

Method B (Quantum-classical hybrid): for each Monte Carlo path simulate forward rates until the second-last alive tenor classically; for the final tenor, load the (conditional) log-normal distribution into n qubits (amplitude encoding), encode the payoff via comparator and Ry rotations, and estimate the expected payoff amplitude using iterative QAE (IQAE); combine quantum-estimated expectation with classical simulated path values to assemble cap price.

Method C (Pure quantum): prepare multivariate amplitude-encoded distribution across registers (nT qubits per maturity, total qubits scales as sum over maturities), encode multi-caplet payoffs via comparator circuits, and apply IQAE to the joint distribution to estimate the cap price directly.

Compare outputs to theoretical Black-76 under LMM; repeat experiments across different numbers of Monte Carlo simulations and different discretization qubit counts; report errors, convergence and confidence intervals.
experiment_process.parameters_and_variations: Monte Carlo sample counts varied (plots show up to ~300 samples); hybrid distribution loading commonly used n = 3 qubits per final tenor in examples; pure-quantum example used up to 18 qubits (3 + 6 + 9 for three caplets) in a demonstration; iterative QAE used to avoid full QFT-based QAE. Experiments repeated (50 trials) to compute average absolute deviation and confidence intervals.

experiment_output.format: Estimated cap prices (scalar), per-method comparisons plotted vs number of Monte Carlo samples; error metrics (absolute estimation error), sample mean and 95% confidence intervals over multiple trials; convergence plots comparing classical MC, hybrid, and pure-quantum approaches against theoretical Black-76 benchmark.
experiment_output.metrics_and_baselines: Metrics: absolute estimation error, average absolute deviation from theoretical value (averaged over 50 trials), sample mean and standard error, convergence behavior vs number of simulations. Baseline: theoretical Black-76 cap price under the LMM (closed-form per-caplet).

key_findings: [supported] The authors implemented a hybrid classical-quantum pipeline that uses classical Monte Carlo (MC) to simulate forward rates up to the second-last tenor and then applies quantum amplitude estimation (QAE/IQAE) to estimate the expectation for the final tenor (caplet payoff).

[supported] In numerical experiments on a benchmark LIBOR Market Model (LMM) cap-pricing example, the quantum-classical hybrid method showed consistently lower estimation error (better convergence) than a pure classical Monte Carlo estimator for the same number of classical MC paths.

[supported] A pure-quantum approach (loading multivariate distributions for all caplets and using QAE end-to-end) requires substantially more qubits and circuit depth; in the presented example a pure-quantum design used 18 qubits to represent three caplets with n=3 per-caplet discretization.

[supported] For small numbers of classical MC samples, the pure-quantum method (as simulated) produced more accurate point estimates than both the hybrid and the pure-classical Monte Carlo methods in some cases, but it is difficult to scale/improve due to circuit-depth and qubit-count requirements.

[supported] Using small register sizes for distribution loading (e.g., n=3 qubits per caplet) can produce discretization bias that becomes more significant for longer maturities (example divergence noted at T=10).

[speculative] Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) offers a quadratic asymptotic speedup over classical Monte Carlo for expectation estimation (cited as background theoretical claim, not newly proved here).
[supported] The authors used an iterative QAE (IQAE) variant to avoid the full inverse quantum Fourier transform, citing implementation-depth considerations.

[supported] Empirical statistics reported: sample mean for a caplet-pricing discretization (n=3) was approximately 2.85e-2 vs theoretical 2.84e-2; discretized vs true lognormal distribution mean and skewness reported (means: 7.391e-2 (discretized) vs 7.406e-2 (true); skewness: 9.33e-4 vs 0.4528).

results_summary: The paper develops and simulates a hybrid classical-quantum workflow to price interest-rate caps under the LIBOR Market Model. Classical Monte Carlo is used to simulate forward rates up to the penultimate tenor and iterative quantum amplitude estimation (IQAE) is applied to estimate the final-tenor caplet expectation. Numerical experiments on benchmark LMM parameters show the hybrid method yields lower estimation errors than pure classical Monte Carlo for the same number of classical samples. A fully quantum (pure-quantum) approach is also constructed in simulation but requires substantially more qubits and circuit depth (e.g., 18 qubits for three caplets with a modest discretization), making it less practical; it can, however, give competitive point estimates for very small sample budgets. The authors discuss discretization bias when using small quantum registers and present theoretical error formulas for classical MC and QAE to motivate the hybrid design.
performance_claims: Pure-quantum circuit in the example: 18 qubits (3 caplets × n=3 per-caplet discretization → 3×(1+2+3)=18 qubits reported in example).
Reported sample standard deviations for pure-quantum experiments across different n: 1.41×10^-3 (n=1), 1.55×10^-3 (n=2), 1.65×10^-3 (n=3).
Sample mean for one pricing experiment: discretized cap price ≈ 2.85×10^-2 vs theoretical Black-76/LMM value ≈ 2.84×10^-2 (n=3 example).
Discretized vs true lognormal distribution statistics for a T=10 example: means 7.391×10^-2 (discretized) vs 7.406×10^-2 (true); skewness 9.33×10^-4 (discretized) vs 0.4528 (true).
Theoretical error scaling cited: classical Monte Carlo error ∝ σ / sqrt(M); QAE error bounds cited ≈ π/M + O(1/M^2) (theoretical formula referenced).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors argue and demonstrate in numerical simulation that applying QAE/IQAE within a hybrid pipeline reduces estimation error versus pure classical Monte Carlo for the same classical sample count. However, they do not demonstrate a measured asymptotic runtime or resource advantage on realistic quantum hardware: the quadratic asymptotic speedup of QAE is a theoretical background claim and practical resource requirements (qubit counts, circuit depth) for full end-to-end quantum implementation are significant. Therefore a concrete, demonstrated quantum advantage in practice is not established and remains speculative.
limitations: Pure quantum method is highly resource intensive: requires a large number of qubits and enormous circuit depth, making it difficult to improve accuracy in practice (author-stated).

The implemented hybrid approach applies QAE only to the final tenor (last caplet) while earlier tenors are handled classically — i.e., only partial quantum acceleration is demonstrated (author-stated).

Discretization/loading of the log-normal distribution with a small number of qubits (e.g., n=3) introduces bias and loss of skewness relative to the true distribution; this degrades accuracy for longer maturities T (author-stated / demonstrated in Appendix F).
Calibration and modeling assumptions: instantaneous volatilities are assumed piecewise-constant (standard practice but a modeling limitation) (author-stated).

Caps pricing in the study ignores joint expectations involving multiple forward rates and therefore does not require modelling correlations; correlation effects are not treated and would be required for more complex derivatives (author-stated).
Use of iterative QAE to avoid full QFT reduces circuit-depth issues but does not eliminate practical resource and depth constraints for large problems (author-stated/in context).

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Integrating iterative quantum amplitude estimation (IQAE) into Monte Carlo for the final tenor demonstrates improved convergence and lower absolute estimation error versus pure classical Monte Carlo in the authors' numerical experiments for cap pricing under the LMM.

#idea:hybrid-approach — A practical hybrid pipeline is proposed: simulate forward rates classically up to the penultimate tenor and apply QAE to the conditional distribution of the final tenor, reducing quantum resource requirements compared to a full joint-quantum approach.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The use of IQAE (avoiding full QFT-based QAE) and small discretization qubit counts (examples with 3–18 qubits) is presented as a path toward near-term NISQ applicability, demonstrated via simulation experiments.

#limitation:qubit-count — The pure-quantum formulation requires qubits that scale with number of maturities and discretization resolution (e.g., example used 18 qubits for 3 caplets), indicating scaling challenges for realistic tenor structures.

#limitation:data-encoding — Amplitude-encoding log-normal distributions and mapping payoffs via comparator circuits and Ry rotations introduces overhead and precision/discretization trade-offs that constrain accuracy and resource demands.
#limitation:simulation-only — All reported experiments are simulation-based (no real QPU hardware results); circuit depths, shot counts, and gate-level resource metrics are not provided.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Reproducibility is limited: no public code or explicit simulator/QPU platform specified and core implementation details (exact gate counts, IQAE sampling parameters) are missing; data are 'available on request' only.
